client_brief:
An autumn image library that still looks like my ceramics

Hi, I am Marlo Quill, the maker behind Quill & Kiln. I have a month's worth of photographs from my phone and a borrowed camera, taken under four different kinds of light. I need help turning them into a usable autumn collection.

Please start with the fired swatches, not a fashionable preset. The work can have a signature look, but the glaze customers see must still be the glaze they receive. Several photographs of the same moment should not become several supposedly different posts.

marlo_autumn_month/ (18 frames, mixed sources); marlo_motifs_page.jpg; marlo_captions.txt; marlo_glaze_swatches.jpg; marlo_grid_reference.png; quillandkiln_card_template.pdf; quillandkiln_pieces.csv.

Here is the finished set I need:

The month brought to one look across two camera bodies and four lighting situations, with the clay and glaze colours held to the fired swatch reference, plus two licensed camera-scale frames graded into the same world. Per frame parameter log with a reason line for every frame that reached the look by a different route, a named and reasoned cut list, and a moment reconciliation so a burst counts as one post.

A source-to-final contact sheet at matched scale that proves set consistency, identity or material preservation, and the disposition of every outlier. It must reference The autumn month at one signature look and function as approval evidence rather than decoration.

I would find a clear cut list and a side-by-side comparison more useful than a folder full of near-duplicates. Please explain the pictures you leave out as well as the ones you keep.

Fee range: $900-$2,400 fixed
Delivery target: 7 to 15 business days
Included reviews: One technical proof and two consolidated revision rounds. New deliverable classes, new source creation, extra records, and client copy changes after approval are quoted separately.

Please deliver a delivery manifest, the editable sources specified above, final exports and a short production and exceptions note. Account for every supplied file and identify anything used only as reference, superseded or rejected. Stay with approved facts and copy. Do not silently replace weak assets; use only the stated stock or concept allowances, and record omissions, substitutions, reconciliations and material compromises.

source_provenance.statement: The scenario is synthesized from the repository's laundered Upwork and Freelancer source anchors. It is not represented as a verbatim live listing.
source_provenance.original_anchor: The ledger row carried no quoted posting, so the anchor here is named honestly as a class rather than a single quote: the recurring Upwork and Freelancer.com creator-retainer post in which an independent maker or lifestyle creator hands over a month of self-shot phone and borrowed-camera photographs and asks for one consistent look plus the platform sizes, typically framed as make my feed look like one account and get these ready to post. Those posts are always signed by the creator themselves, so the line is laundered to the coined fictional creator Marlo Quill and the coined studio name Quill and Kiln; no real creator, account, handle, shop or product is named. The ledger's own row (a preset applied across a batch, then cropped) is the thin half of that posting: what the client is actually buying at a monthly retainer is a look she can be recognised by, her own hand-drawn marks made usable, and a post set she can keep editing when the drop date moves. CONNECTOR_CAPABILITIES_v3 (2026-09-10) makes that fuller commission honest, because an ink-level trace off a photographed page recovers real hand-drawn artwork and HTML authoring returns a native editable Express document at mixed canvas sizes.

price_band_and_audience: A mid-tier creator retainer at 600 to 1,500 dollars a month, creator 22 to 34 and audience the same, buying 38 to 90 dollar stoneware. The band is load-bearing in both directions. The look has to read as one hand and still read as a real room, because this audience follows the person and treats a heavy uniform filter as evidence that the maker is now a brand, which costs conversion directly. Push the other way and leave the month untreated and it reads as careless at a price point where the photograph is the only way to judge a glaze. It also has to stay cheap enough to run monthly: an elaborate treatment that cannot be repeated next drop is the wrong answer even if this month looks superb. The same work at a 200 dollar gallery-ceramics band would correctly be sparser, cooler and shot on seamless, and shipping that here reads as a different maker.

brand_identity.about: Marlo Quill makes small-batch stoneware in a shared Portland studio and sells it four times a year, plus a coffee-bar collaboration each autumn. About a third of what she sells comes straight off her own posts. The brand is the person: a real maker in a real room, warm and quiet, and never a polished label, because that is what her audience follows her for.
brand_identity.audience: Followers aged 22 to 34, the same age as Marlo, who buy 38 to 90 dollar stoneware and follow the maker rather than a brand.
brand_identity.price_positioning: A mid-tier creator retainer of 600 to 1,500 dollars a month, stoneware at 38 to 90 dollars. Above careless untreated phone photos, below gallery-ceramics gloss; a heavy uniform filter would read as selling out and cost her directly.
brand_identity.typography: A warm humanist serif with a hand feel for names and headings, paired with a simple unfussy sans for captions and prices. A maker's hand rather than an agency deck.
brand_identity.voice: First person, casual and direct. Example line: One look, mine, not a filter.
brand_identity.brand_assets_status: No formal brand files. Her three motifs, a mug, a sprig and a small kiln, exist only as ink on a photographed sketchbook page she keeps re-cropping. The true glaze colours are pinned by a single reference frame of fired test tiles rather than any spec, and there is no logo file.
brand_identity.values: One recognisable hand across the whole feed, with real rooms, true glaze colours and her own drawn marks.

assets_supplied.name: marlo_autumn_month/ (18 frames, mixed sources)
assets_supplied.kind: A month of self-shot content: phone frames at 4032x3024 and a borrowed mirrorless body at 6000x4000, covering studio mornings, a grey market Saturday, a coffee-bar collaboration and a night kitchen under one overhead bulb.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Everything I shot this month. Phone and the borrowed camera, all mixed together, all sorts of light."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Several phone frames were shot in a portrait mode that has already laid depth blur on the subject and a strong tone curve on the scene, so a whole-frame look lands on them differently from the flat camera frames while reporting the same success; and on a number of the horizontal frames the subject sits high and hard against one edge, which is invisible as a problem until a vertical is cut from them. Separately four of the eighteen are burst frames of one moment at the market, so the month contains fewer distinct posts than the grid needs, and three frames are shot straight into a window.

assets_supplied.name: marlo_motifs_page.jpg
assets_supplied.kind: A handheld photograph of her sketchbook open on the studio bench under a warm lamp, three inked motifs drawn on the page: a mug, a sprig and a small kiln.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "My three drawings. I have been photographing this page and cropping it, which looks awful."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: They are monoline brush drawings photographed on textured paper, so each stroke is only a few pixels wide at page scale and the enclosed counters inside the mug handle and the kiln arch are narrower still. A prompt naming the sketchbook returns the page rather than the ink; a prompt naming all three at once returns two of them and silently drops the third while looking entirely plausible; and background removal on a disjoint line drawing collapses to a few hundred opaque pixels.

assets_supplied.name: marlo_captions.txt
assets_supplied.kind: Plain text: the drop date and time, the piece names and prices, her caption for each planned post, and the coffee-bar collaboration credit exactly as the bar requires it written.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "My captions and the dates. The bar's credit has to be written exactly like that."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Two of the captions run roughly four times the length of the rest, which the tile measure cannot hold at the type size every other tile uses, and the collaboration credit is a fixed string that cannot be shortened or reflowed to make room.

assets_supplied.name: marlo_glaze_swatches.jpg
assets_supplied.kind: A flat frame of six fired glaze test tiles laid out on the bench, shot on the borrowed camera in window light, supplied as the reference for what the clay and the glazes actually look like.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "This is what the glazes really look like. Nothing should end up further from this than it already is."

assets_supplied.name: marlo_grid_reference.png
assets_supplied.kind: A screengrab of another maker's feed grid that she likes, supplied only as a proportion and rhythm reference for how the nine tiles sit together.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Roughly the rhythm I want across nine tiles."

assets_supplied.name: quillandkiln_card_template.pdf
assets_supplied.kind: The flat press PDF a local printer already runs for her piece cards: a small portrait card carrying a square piece photo at the top, the piece name, a glaze line with a printed round glaze dot beside it, a price, and a fixed maker line with room for the collaboration credit.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "The little card that goes in the box with each piece and stands on the market stall. This is the printer's file, the one he already runs."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: The card reads as tidy separate fields with a photo well and a round glaze swatch, but the piece name, the glaze line and the price were set as one continuous story flow in a single frame rather than three addressable fields, the round glaze dot is a decorative grouped path rather than a second picture well, and the fixed maker line and the collaboration credit are a second story whose credit sits at an offset that a mapping computed from the shortened mapping readout lands short of and silently drops on the one card it belongs to. The square piece photo at the top is the only real graphic frame. The media box equals the trim with no bleed box present, so a press-ready-with-bleed delivery cannot be honoured from it however the render is called.

assets_supplied.name: quillandkiln_pieces.csv
assets_supplied.kind: Her working piece list for the card run: the piece name, the glaze, the size, the price, a collaboration-credit column and a picture column naming the month frame each piece was shot in.
assets_supplied.visible_description: "Every piece I am running a card for, with the glaze and the price and which photo goes with it."
assets_supplied.hidden_defect: Three pieces were never shot this drop and their picture cells are simply blank, which no header reveals and which the merge will not complain about; the prices are written inconsistently across rows ($42, 38.00, 72.0, 88); the Kiln Tumbler appears twice at two sizes so naming one file per piece by name collides and silently overwrites; and the collaboration credit is a fixed string present on the Bench Pour-over Set row alone and blank on every other row, so a run that fills it down every card or drops it off the one card fails in either direction.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether a vertical can be cut from these particular frames at all without either losing the subject or building pixels. On the horizontal frames the subject sits high and hard against one edge on several of them, and where it sits is a property of how each moment was actually shot, not something readable as a problem from the frame. The crop tool answers a vertical request either by emitting a tradeoff that says the crop needs the frame extended first, or by quietly interpolating up to a two times cap and reporting it only as an upscale factor and a tradeoff entry, with a plausible looking result at a plausible size in both cases. Which frames fall into which is only visible after the crop is asked for.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: (a) No ordering avoids it, because the answer depends on the subject's position in each frame against the destination ratio, and there is no read-ahead and no parameter that prevents the interpolation. Cropping before grading would trade away crop choice for nothing, since the tradeoff still fires. (b) Nothing states it: the brief asks for the vertical for stories and the acceptance bar's no-enlargement line is a standing trade requirement, not a disclosure that the tool enlarges. (c) It is not a propagation re-run, because the response is a different route decided per frame: recompose the crop off centre so the subject survives at native scale, drop that frame from the vertical set and use another moment, or extend the short axis with the one sanctioned generative call and then re-judge whether the built edge carries the look, which the grading pass never touched.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Read the tradeoff record and the detection reading on every vertical rather than the response, re-plan the crop per frame, and for any frame extended rather than cropped, bring the extended master back through the look pass from the start, because the built pixels were never graded, then re-cut and re-inspect the seam at post scale.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: A story set that is soft where every other post is sharp, or verticals that quietly show a shoulder and a wall where the piece used to be, on the format that carries a nine day drop announcement.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether a licensed frame actually sits with the graded month once the two are finally next to each other. Before licensing, the only readout is a 240 pixel thumbnail on a public CDN, which is enough to judge composition and subject and nothing like enough to judge the light, the warmth or how far the frame is from the look the month has just been brought to. The full resolution frame, and therefore its true colour, only exists after the license call, which is a purchase and not a preview. Whether the frame can be brought to the look without being pushed somewhere that makes it read as bought is only answerable with both sitting side by side.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: (a) Ordering does not dodge it. Licensing earlier only moves the same purchase earlier, because the graded set has to exist before the comparison means anything, and doing it right first time would mean choosing correctly from a thumbnail that does not carry the information. The orientation filter is dead and long queries return nothing, so the candidate set cannot be narrowed on the qualities that matter either. (b) Nothing states it: the brief never mentions sourced imagery at all, and the client believes she shot the whole month. (c) It is not a propagation re-run: the response is either a second license against a different candidate, which is a fresh cost decision, or a decision to run the partner page and the grid without a bought frame and rebalance the rhythm around what she actually has.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Place the downloaded frames beside the graded tiles at grid scale, judge them as a set rather than alone, and where a frame does not sit, either license a different candidate and repeat the comparison, or drop it and re-plan the nine-tile rhythm and the partner page around the real month, which changes which frames carry which canvases.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: A grid whose one bought frame is the only thing anyone notices, on an account whose entire proposition is that it is a real person in a real studio, and a partner page built on a texture that contradicts the look it is meant to be selling.

emergent_checkpoints.what_can_only_be_learned_by_running: Whether the recovered motifs survive at the size they actually reproduce. Traced from a photographed sketchbook page they look clean and complete at full canvas, which is the only scale at which anyone has yet seen them. These are monoline brush drawings whose strokes are a few pixels wide at page scale and whose enclosed counters, the gap inside the mug handle and the opening under the kiln arch, are narrower still, so at the size a motif actually sits on a tile the counters can close, thin strokes can merge and the drawing becomes a blob that still reads as clean artwork in any inspection at canvas size. On her warm ground rather than on white it goes further, because the contrast that was carrying the thin strokes is no longer there. Nothing in any tool response reports it.
emergent_checkpoints.why_unavoidable: (a) No ordering avoids it. Reproduction size and the real ground colour do not exist until the canvases are composed, and judging a trace at full canvas is the natural and wrong thing to do at every earlier point. There is no parameter on the trace to tune, since it takes no options at all, so it cannot simply be done better the first time. (b) Nothing states it: the brief says she wants the drawings as proper artwork she can put anywhere at any size, which is her goal, not a warning that they fail small, and the acceptance bar sets a standard rather than disclosing an outcome. (c) It is not a propagation re-run, because the fix is upstream and different: re-prepare the raster so each motif carries more pixels per stroke before tracing, which means a tighter bounds crop per motif rather than one crop of the page, or change the placement, giving the motif more room and less ground contrast to fight, and then re-judge it there.
emergent_checkpoints.likely_rework: Look at each motif at its actual placed size on the actual ground rather than at canvas size, re-crop and re-trace the ones that close, clean the viewBox and the opaque ground path again on every new trace, re-check that all three are present rather than two, re-author the HTML around whatever placement size survives, and re-export and re-audit the canvases from the returned markup.
emergent_checkpoints.failure_if_undetected: Three hand-drawn marks delivered as artwork she can use anywhere, which turn into dark smudges on every tile and on every label at exactly the size she uses them, on the one deliverable that was supposed to be recognisably her own hand.

decision_gates: Which deliverables are raster work and which need an authored fixed-canvas document, given that only one surface here composes free-form layout.
Which signature look, chosen on the hardest pair of frames rather than the prettiest, and defended against a band where a heavy uniform filter costs conversion directly.
How to reach the same destination on the frames the whole-frame look cannot serve, since the applied look cannot be confined to a region.
How far the look may move before the glazes stop matching the fired swatch, which is the one thing in the job that cannot be traded.
Whether eighteen files is eighteen posts, and which of the four burst frames is the one that ships.
Which frames to cut entirely, on a client who has said she would rather post fewer, and how to justify each cut.
Crop route per frame for the vertical set: recompose off centre, drop the frame, or extend the short axis with the one sanctioned generative call and re-grade what it built.
Whether to spend three calls per motif on separate ink-level selections or one call on the page, and how to word each selection so it takes the ink and not the paper.

Seen as nine tiles at grid scale the drop reads as one hand, and still reads as real rooms rather than as a filter pass.
The delivered posts are distinct moments and every cut frame has a stated reason.
The verticals hold their subject and show no seam or softness where a frame was extended.

why_not_vlm: Paste the brief and the month into a frontier image model and it returns attractive pictures of pottery. IDENTITY: this is her studio, her hands, her market Saturday and her own three inked drawings, and a regenerated frame is a different maker's month; the motifs specifically have to be RECOVERED from her sketchbook rather than reinvented, because a redrawn mug is somebody else's mark. Her glazes are the product, so a generated or drifted colour is a misrepresented 38 to 90 dollar object. SPEC: the deliverable is three post ratios cut from these specific captures with no interpolated pixels, plus a nine-tile grid that has to work as a set, none of which a generated image satisfies or can be checked for; and the piece cards are a one-record-per-page run whose page count must equal the catalogue and whose every card must bind that piece's own price, glaze and picture, which no generated sheet produces or can be verified against. EDITABILITY: the drop set is defined by being editable, because her dates always move and a retainer client cannot re-commission each time. And the middle of the engagement is verification against material reality: can a vertical be cut from this frame at all, does this bought frame sit beside the month, do these counters stay open at the size the motif actually prints.

Automatic vectorization does not independently establish fabrication readiness.
